taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes it was formerly considered conspecific with Boat-tailed Grackle (Q. major), but sympatry without interbreeding is known from Louisiana to Texas (AOU 1998).
fieldMarks: Very long tail and yellow eyes; male 46-58 cm, female 38-46 cm
Male glossy black, more evenly coloured than Common Grackle and much larger
Female buff below and on the eyebrow, smaller than the male
behavior: Usually feeds in flocks, mostly on the ground or wading in very shallow water; also forages in trees and shrubs, searching for nests to rob
Omnivorous: insects, spiders, crayfish, tadpoles, small fish, lizards, eggs and nestlings, plus seeds, waste grain, berries and fruit
Variety of whistles, clucks and hissing notes; breeding range is expanding
habitat: Groves, thickets, farms, towns and city parks; mostly lowlands including farmland, marshes, irrigated fields, suburban lawns and brushy areas; avoids true desert but occurs around streams or ponds in dry country.
range: Resident from southeastern California and southern Nevada east to southern Nebraska and southwestern Missouri, south into South America; breeding range is expanding, with recent nesting in Oregon and probably Idaho.

lookalikes.name: Common grackle
lookalikes.howToTell: Smaller with a shorter tail and less evenly coloured male.

lookalikes.name: Boat-tailed grackle
lookalikes.howToTell: Audubon says to compare; NatureServe treats it as a separate species with overlap from Louisiana to Texas.
